---
title: "NAF — Multi-level classification"
---

This page compares against the [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd) baseline, described on its own page.

The five-level hierarchy of NAF 2025 opens a natural multi-task training strategy: rather than predicting only the finest level (sub-class), the model can be trained to simultaneously predict multiple levels of the hierarchy. Two theoretical benefits follow: (1) coarser levels are easier to classify and inject additional gradient signal that guides the shared representation towards features discriminant across the taxonomy; (2) at inference time the model directly outputs predictions at every level, requiring no post-hoc aggregation.

All five NAF levels are used: the **section** (1 letter, 20 codes in the training set out of 21 in the full nomenclature), the **division** (first 2 characters, 84 out of 87), the **group** (first 3 characters, 274 out of 287), the **class** (first 4 characters, 586 out of 651), and the **sub-class** (full 5-character code, 679 out of 747). All five classification heads share a single **TokenEmbedder** — one WordPiece tokenizer and one embedding matrix — that is jointly optimised through the sum of five independent cross-entropy losses. Each level then has its own **SentenceEmbedder** (either mean pooling or label attention) and a **ClassificationHead** (a single linear projection). This design keeps the parameter count modest: only the five separate sentence embedders and linear heads add level-specific parameters on top of the shared trunk. The architecture natively supports additional categorical input variables; they are not used here for simplicity, as the NAF dataset provides only a free-text description.

**A word of caution on "independent": the five heads never talk to each other.** Nothing forces the section, division, group, class, and sub-class predictions for the same example to be mutually consistent — they are five separate softmaxes over five separate label spaces, each optimised against its own ground truth, with no shared constraint tying them to the same underlying NAF code. On [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd), by contrast, only the sub-class is ever predicted, and every coarser level is a deterministic truncation of that one code — so its levels are *always* mutually consistent by construction, and can never disagree with each other. Here, they can, and do: it is entirely possible for the division head to land on the correct division while the section head (independently) misses, even though the true division determines the true section — an outcome that is mathematically impossible under truncation. This isn't a flaw to fix; it's the entire point of giving each level its own head — but the five predictions shown anywhere on this page should be read as independent opinions, not a single coherent decision. Sharing one token encoder trained on the sum of all five losses could still nudge the heads toward agreeing in practice; whether it actually does is an empirical question the results further down answer directly.

## Hyperparameter sweep

Architecture is fixed here (`n_layers=0`, i.e. FastText-style mean pooling — the multi-level trainer does not yet expose the FATE transformer variant), so the sweep covers `embedding_dim` in {64, 128, 256, 512} × `vocab_size` in {2000, 5000, 10000, 20000} × `n_heads_label_attention` in {none, 4} × `lr` in {0.0005, 0.001} — `lr=0.0001` was dropped from this grid, giving 4 × 4 × 2 × 2 = **64 runs** per `train_fraction` rather than 96. As with the [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd) page, the `naf_multilevel` MLflow experiment mixes four `train_fraction` sweeps over the same grid: **0.13**, **0.26**, **0.52**, and **1.0**. The rest of this section uses **1.0** only (the full, largest sweep) — the figure below is the exception, comparing all four to isolate the effect of training-data size itself.

```{python}
#| label: fetch-mlflow-naf-multilevel

from pathlib import Path
import mlflow
import pandas as pd

RENAME_COLS_ML = {
    "params.embedding_dim":            "emb_dim",
    "params.vocab_size":               "vocab_size",
    "params.n_heads_label_attention":  "n_heads_label_attn",
    "params.lr":                       "lr",
    "metrics.num_params":              "num_params",
    "metrics.train_time_s":            "train_time_s",
    "metrics.val_loss":                "min_val_loss",
    "metrics.test_accuracy_sec":       "test_accuracy_sec",
    "metrics.test_accuracy_div":       "test_accuracy_div",
    "metrics.test_accuracy_grp":       "test_accuracy_grp",
    "metrics.test_accuracy_cls":       "test_accuracy_cls",
    "metrics.test_accuracy_sub":       "test_accuracy_sub",
    "metrics.test_f1_macro_sec":       "test_f1_macro_sec",
    "metrics.test_f1_macro_div":       "test_f1_macro_div",
    "metrics.test_f1_macro_grp":       "test_f1_macro_grp",
    "metrics.test_f1_macro_cls":       "test_f1_macro_cls",
    "metrics.test_f1_macro_sub":       "test_f1_macro_sub",
}
KEY_COLS_ML = ["emb_dim", "vocab_size", "n_heads_label_attn", "lr"]

def arch_label_ml(row):
    la = str(row["n_heads_label_attn"]) == "4"
    return "FastText + Label Attention" if la else "FastText"

def fetch_runs_ml(experiment_name: str, cache_path: Path, train_fraction: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    cache_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    if cache_path.exists():
        return pd.read_csv(cache_path)
    raw = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=[experiment_name], max_results=5000)
    raw = raw[raw["status"] == "FINISHED"].copy()
    raw = raw[pd.to_numeric(raw["params.train_fraction"], errors="coerce") == train_fraction]
    raw = raw.rename(columns={k: v for k, v in RENAME_COLS_ML.items() if k in raw.columns})
    for col in ["emb_dim", "vocab_size"]:
        raw[col] = pd.to_numeric(raw[col], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
    raw["lr"]         = raw["lr"].astype(float)
    raw["num_params"] = pd.to_numeric(raw["num_params"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
    raw["architecture"] = raw.apply(arch_label_ml, axis=1)
    raw = raw.sort_values("min_val_loss").drop_duplicates(subset=KEY_COLS_ML, keep="first")
    raw.to_csv(cache_path, index=False)
    return raw

# train_fraction=0.13 — earliest, smallest sweep
df_ml_frac13 = fetch_runs_ml("naf_multilevel", Path("results/naf_multilevel/runs_frac13.csv"), train_fraction=0.13)

# train_fraction=0.26 — intermediate sweep
df_ml_frac26 = fetch_runs_ml("naf_multilevel", Path("results/naf_multilevel/runs_frac26.csv"), train_fraction=0.26)

# train_fraction=0.52 — third sweep
df_ml_frac52 = fetch_runs_ml("naf_multilevel", Path("results/naf_multilevel/runs_frac52.csv"), train_fraction=0.52)

# train_fraction=1.0 — full usable set, the latest and largest sweep — used as the main dataset below
df_ml_frac100 = fetch_runs_ml("naf_multilevel", Path("results/naf_multilevel/runs_frac100.csv"), train_fraction=1.0)

df_ml = df_ml_frac100
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-trainsize-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Validation loss vs. training set size, by architecture"

import plotly.graph_objects as go

COLORS_ML = {
    "FastText":                          "#2196F3",
    "FastText + Label Attention":        "#00BCD4",
}
N_TRAIN_ML = {0.13: 163615, 0.26: 327230, 0.52: 654461, 1.0: 1208579}

means13  = df_ml_frac13.groupby("architecture")["min_val_loss"].mean()
means26  = df_ml_frac26.groupby("architecture")["min_val_loss"].mean()
means52  = df_ml_frac52.groupby("architecture")["min_val_loss"].mean()
means100 = df_ml_frac100.groupby("architecture")["min_val_loss"].mean()

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in COLORS_ML:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[N_TRAIN_ML[0.13], N_TRAIN_ML[0.26], N_TRAIN_ML[0.52], N_TRAIN_ML[1.0]],
        y=[means13[arch], means26[arch], means52[arch], means100[arch]],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch,
        line=dict(color=COLORS_ML[arch], width=2), marker=dict(size=9),
        hovertemplate="train size=%{x:,}<br>mean val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Training set size", yaxis_title="Mean validation loss",
    xaxis=dict(
        tickvals=[N_TRAIN_ML[0.13], N_TRAIN_ML[0.26], N_TRAIN_ML[0.52], N_TRAIN_ML[1.0]],
        ticktext=["163,615", "327,230", "654,461", "1,208,579"],
    ),
    legend_title="Architecture", height=430,
)
fig.show()
```

Growing the training data (163,615 → 327,230 → 654,461 → 1,208,579 examples) steadily improves mean validation loss for both architectures — FastText from ≈0.537 to ≈0.491 to ≈0.457 to ≈0.439, FastText + Label Attention from ≈0.723 to ≈0.591 to ≈0.492 to ≈0.440 — with the label-attention variant benefiting more at each step, the same pattern as [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd): the gap between the two architectures narrows from ≈0.186 at 163,615 examples to ≈0.100 at 327,230 to ≈0.035 at 654,461 to essentially **zero** (≈0.002) at 1,208,579, as label attention gets enough examples per class to learn meaningful per-class query vectors — here shared jointly across five hierarchy levels rather than one — and fully closes the gap with plain FastText once the full training set is used.

### Capacity & robustness

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Val loss vs. parameters

```{python}
#| label: fig-pareto-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Validation loss vs. number of parameters"

ARCHS_PRESENT_ML = [a for a in COLORS_ML if a in df_ml["architecture"].unique()]

df_ml_curves = (
    df_ml.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size", "num_params"], as_index=False)
    ["min_val_loss"].min()
    .sort_values("num_params")
)

fig = go.Figure()

for arch in ARCHS_PRESENT_ML:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers",
        name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=True,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS_ML[arch], size=8, opacity=1.0),
    ))

for arch, group in df_ml.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["num_params"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(arch, "grey"), size=5, opacity=0.3),
        hovertemplate="params=%{x:,}<br>val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

for arch, group in df_ml_curves.groupby("architecture"):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=group["num_params"], y=group["min_val_loss"],
        mode="lines+markers", name=arch, legendgroup=arch, showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(arch, "grey"), width=2), marker=dict(size=5),
        hovertemplate="params=%{x:,}<br>best val_loss=%{y:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

y_cap_ml = df_ml["min_val_loss"].quantile(0.95)
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of parameters",
    yaxis_title="Validation loss",
    legend_title="Architecture",
    height=450,
    xaxis=dict(tickformat=".2s"),
    yaxis=dict(range=[df_ml["min_val_loss"].min() * 0.98, y_cap_ml]),
)
fig.show()
```

As on the single-level page, there's no clean pareto frontier — `num_params` mixes together `vocab_size` and `emb_dim`, whose individual effects pull in different directions (see the interaction heatmap further down). Label attention is on par with FastText on average here (≈0.441 vs. ≈0.439, a ≈0.002 gap — statistically indistinguishable) and its best configuration even beats FastText's best (≈0.417 vs. ≈0.426). But it's noisier: at its largest configuration (`emb_dim`=512, `vocab_size`=20000, ≈16.3M params) it spikes to the worst validation loss of either architecture (≈0.467), reproduced across both runs there — extra capacity seems to overfit rather than help.

#### Stability


FastText is also more stable: its results cluster tightly (std ≈0.0081) while Label Attention spreads almost twice as wide (std ≈0.0150) — the same direction as the single-level page. Medians are nearly identical (≈0.439 vs. ≈0.440), so this spread, not the average, is what separates the two architectures here.

Label attention trains dramatically **slower** here — mean ≈53,930s (≈15.0h) vs. ≈9,520s (≈2.6h) for FastText, roughly a 5.7× gap: five heads sharing one label-attention-driven sentence embedder mean five times the cross-attention computation per forward pass, and with a full training set to keep improving on, the run rarely stops early, paying that per-step cost for the whole training budget.

### Interaction: embedding dimension × vocabulary size

```{python}
#| label: fig-heatmap-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Mean validation loss by embedding dimension and vocabulary size"

import numpy as np
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

vmin_ml = df_ml.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean().min()
vmax_ml = df_ml.groupby(["architecture", "emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean().max()

n_cols_hm_ml = min(2, len(ARCHS_PRESENT_ML))
n_rows_hm_ml = (len(ARCHS_PRESENT_ML) + n_cols_hm_ml - 1) // n_cols_hm_ml
fig = make_subplots(rows=n_rows_hm_ml, cols=n_cols_hm_ml, subplot_titles=ARCHS_PRESENT_ML,
                    horizontal_spacing=0.08, vertical_spacing=0.28)

for idx, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_PRESENT_ML):
    row, col = divmod(idx, n_cols_hm_ml)
    pivot = (
        df_ml[df_ml["architecture"] == arch]
        .groupby(["emb_dim", "vocab_size"])["min_val_loss"].mean()
        .unstack("vocab_size")
        .reindex(index=emb_vals_ml, columns=vocab_vals_ml)
    )
    x_labels = [f"{v // 1000}k" for v in vocab_vals_ml]
    y_labels = [str(v) for v in emb_vals_ml]

    is_dark = (pivot.values - vmin_ml) / (vmax_ml - vmin_ml) > 0.65
    for mask, text_color, show_scale in [(~is_dark, "#333333", idx == 0), (is_dark, "#ffffff", False)]:
        z_masked = np.where(mask, pivot.values, np.nan)
        fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
            z=z_masked,
            x=x_labels,
            y=y_labels,
            colorscale="Viridis_r",
            zmin=vmin_ml, zmax=vmax_ml,
            text=[[f"{v:.3f}" if not np.isnan(v) else "" for v in row_] for row_ in z_masked],
            texttemplate="%{text}",
            textfont=dict(color=text_color),
            showscale=show_scale,
            colorbar=dict(title="Mean val loss", orientation="h", x=0.5, xanchor="center",
                          y=-0.38, yanchor="top", len=0.5, thickness=18, title_side="bottom") if show_scale else None,
            hovertemplate="vocab=%{x}<br>emb_dim=%{y}<br>val_loss=%{z:.4f}<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
        ), row=row + 1, col=col + 1)
    fig.update_yaxes(
        title_text="Embedding dim" if col == 0 else "",
        range=[-0.5, len(y_labels) - 0.5], row=row + 1, col=col + 1,
    )
    fig.update_xaxes(
        title_text="Vocabulary size", title_font=dict(size=12), tickangle=0,
        range=[-0.5, len(x_labels) - 0.5], row=row + 1, col=col + 1,
    )
    xaxis_id = "x" if idx == 0 else f"x{idx + 1}"
    fig.update_yaxes(scaleanchor=xaxis_id, scaleratio=1, constrain="domain", row=row + 1, col=col + 1)
    fig.update_xaxes(constrain="domain", row=row + 1, col=col + 1)

for ann in fig.layout.annotations:
    ann.update(font=dict(size=12))
fig.update_layout(height=500, width=790, margin=dict(l=50, r=20, t=40, b=130))
fig.show()
```

FastText is fairly flat across the grid — best cell (emb_dim=128, vocab=10,000, 0.430) and worst (emb_dim=64, vocab=2,000, 0.455) are close together. Label Attention is more sensitive, but not uniformly: at emb_dim=64, growing the vocab from 2,000 to 20,000 barely moves the loss (0.450→0.458, a 0.008 swing), while the same vocab change at emb_dim=512 swings much more (0.440→0.463, a 0.022 swing) — the single worst cell in the whole grid. A larger token embedder doesn't buy label attention robustness to vocabulary size here; if anything it makes the model more sensitive to it.

## Prediction analysis and comparison with single-level

This section examines what the models actually predict, using the same two architectures as [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd) — `FastText` and `FastText + Label Attention`. For each architecture, the model is the single run from the hyperparameter sweep above with the best **sub-class** test accuracy — not the lowest overall (weighted) validation loss used to pick "best" in the sweep analysis — since sub-class is the finest, most demanding level and the one directly comparable to the single-level page. Unlike that page, exact-match accuracy on the 679 sub-classes is not the only thing available here: the model predicts all five hierarchy levels **directly**, through five independent classification heads sharing one token encoder, rather than deriving coarser levels by truncating a single sub-class prediction. On the single-level page, only the sub-class code is predicted (e.g. `6820G`); the coarser levels are never predicted themselves, just mechanically cut from that one string (`code[:2]` for the division, `code[:4]` for the class, etc.). Here, each level gets its own dedicated prediction, so — unlike a truncated code, which is right at every coarser level whenever the sub-class is right — the five levels can disagree with each other (e.g. a correct section with a wrong sub-class).

```{python}
#| label: load-predictions-naf-multilevel

import json
import urllib.request
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import HTML

PRED_BUCKET_ML = "https://minio.lab.sspcloud.fr/projet-text-classif/predictions/naf_multilevel"
ARCH_FILES_ML  = {
    "FastText":                   "fasttext.npz",
    "FastText + Label Attention": "fasttext_labatt.npz",
}
LEVEL_NAMES     = ["sec", "div", "grp", "cls", "sub"]
LEVEL_LABELS_ML = {"sec": "Section", "div": "Division", "grp": "Group", "cls": "Class", "sub": "Sub-class"}
NAF_PARQUET_URL = "https://minio.lab.sspcloud.fr/projet-text-classif/datasets/naf_merged.parquet"

PREDS_DIR_ML = Path("results/naf_multilevel/preds")
PREDS_DIR_ML.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

preds_by_arch_ml = {}   # arch -> {"y_test": (N,5), "y_pred_<level>": (N,)}
for arch, fname in ARCH_FILES_ML.items():
    cache = PREDS_DIR_ML / fname
    try:
        if not cache.exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{PRED_BUCKET_ML}/{fname}", cache)
        d = np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
        preds_by_arch_ml[arch] = {"y_test": d["y_test"].astype(int)}
        preds_by_arch_ml[arch].update({
            f"y_pred_{lvl}": d[f"y_pred_{lvl}"].astype(int) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES
        })
    except Exception:
        pass

ARCHS_AVAIL_ML = list(preds_by_arch_ml.keys())

# The npz predictions only carry integer-encoded labels, not raw text or NAF codes.
# Both are fully reconstructible offline: the test split (seed=42, val_size=
# test_size=50000, independent of train_fraction since only the train split is
# subsampled) and the per-level label encoders (fit on the full deduplicated
# corpus) are deterministic — see src/multilevel/naf_data.py::load_naf. Cached
# here so this only re-downloads/re-fits once.
classes_cache = PREDS_DIR_ML / "level_classes.json"
if classes_cache.exists():
    LEVEL_CLASSES = json.loads(classes_cache.read_text())
else:
    df_full_ml = pd.read_parquet(NAF_PARQUET_URL, columns=["libelle_cleaned"] + LEVEL_NAMES).dropna()
    LEVEL_CLASSES = {lvl: sorted(df_full_ml[lvl].astype(str).unique().tolist()) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES}
    classes_cache.write_text(json.dumps(LEVEL_CLASSES))

test_cache = PREDS_DIR_ML / "test_reconstruction.parquet"
if test_cache.exists():
    df_test_ml = pd.read_parquet(test_cache)
else:
    df_full_ml = pd.read_parquet(NAF_PARQUET_URL, columns=["libelle_cleaned"] + LEVEL_NAMES)
    df_full_ml = df_full_ml.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)
    df_full_ml = df_full_ml.sample(frac=1, random_state=42).reset_index(drop=True)
    df_test_ml = df_full_ml.iloc[len(df_full_ml) - 50000:].reset_index(drop=True)
    df_test_ml.to_parquet(test_cache)

X_TEST_ML = df_test_ml["libelle_cleaned"].values

with open("assets/naf2025_structure.json") as f:
    _naf_struct_ml = json.load(f)
SECTION_LABEL_ML    = {s["id"]: s["label"] for s in _naf_struct_ml["sections"]}
SECTION_COLOR_ML     = {s["id"]: s["color"] for s in _naf_struct_ml["sections"]}
SOUSCLASSE_LABEL_ML = _naf_struct_ml["sousclasses"]  # keyed like "01.11Y"

def code_of(level: str, idx: int) -> str:
    return LEVEL_CLASSES[level][idx]

def label_of(level: str, code: str) -> str:
    # Only sections and sub-classes carry a human-readable label in
    # naf2025_structure.json — division/group/class entries only reference
    # their children, so those levels fall back to the bare code.
    if level == "sec":
        return SECTION_LABEL_ML.get(code, code)
    if level == "sub":
        dotted = code[:2] + "." + code[2:]
        return SOUSCLASSE_LABEL_ML.get(dotted, code)
    return code
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Accuracy vs. class support

Same question as on the single-level page, restricted to the finest (**sub-class**) head: **do errors concentrate in the sub-classes with the fewest training examples?**

```{python}
#| label: fig-support-acc-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Per-sub-class accuracy vs. number of test examples for that sub-class (log x-axis)"

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML:
    d = preds_by_arch_ml[arch]
    y_test_sub = d["y_test"][:, 4]
    y_pred_sub = d["y_pred_sub"]
    classes_present = np.unique(y_test_sub)
    support_a  = np.array([(y_test_sub == c).sum() for c in classes_present])
    accuracy_a = np.array([(y_pred_sub[y_test_sub == c] == c).mean() for c in classes_present])
    hover_codes  = [code_of("sub", c) for c in classes_present]
    hover_labels = [label_of("sub", c) for c in hover_codes]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=support_a, y=accuracy_a * 100, mode="markers", name=arch,
        marker=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(arch, "grey"), size=6, opacity=0.55,
                    line=dict(width=0.5, color="white")),
        customdata=np.stack([hover_codes, hover_labels], axis=1),
        hovertemplate="<b>%{customdata[0]} — %{customdata[1]}</b><br>"
                      "test support=%{x}<br>accuracy=%{y:.1f}%<extra>" + arch + "</extra>",
    ))

TICK_VALS_ML = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000]
TICK_TEXT_ML = ["1", "2", "5", "10", "20", "50", "100", "200", "500", "1k", "2k", "5k"]

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Test-set support for this sub-class (log scale)",
    yaxis_title="Accuracy on this sub-class (%)",
    xaxis=dict(type="log", tickvals=TICK_VALS_ML, ticktext=TICK_TEXT_ML),
    yaxis=dict(range=[-2, 102]),
    legend_title="Architecture", height=450,
)
fig.show()
```

The same funnel shape as on the single-level page: 311 of the 513 sub-classes present in the test set have fewer than 20 test examples, and their accuracy swings across the entire 0–100% range; the 50 sub-classes with 200+ examples tighten into a 56–100% band (mean ≈89%). Sharing the token encoder with four auxiliary heads doesn't change this — sub-class accuracy is still driven by how much data that specific sub-class has, not by the auxiliary supervision.

### Hierarchical accuracy

An earlier version of this section derived every coarser level by truncating the **sub-class head**'s prediction, exactly like [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd) is forced to (it has no separate section/division/group/class head to ask). That method turned out to be misleading here: the multi-level model has four genuinely **independent** auxiliary heads, each trained with its own cross-entropy loss, and they are *not* reducible to a truncation of the sub-class guess. Checking directly — among examples where the sub-class head is wrong, how often is the **independent section head** still correct — gives 61.4–61.5%, against only 52.4–53.0% from truncating the (wrong) sub-class guess. The charts below query each head directly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hierarchy-direct-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Error rate by hierarchy level: multi-level's independent heads vs. single-level's truncated cascade"

level_acc_ml = {}  # arch -> [acc at sec, div, grp, cls, sub], each from its own head
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML:
    d = preds_by_arch_ml[arch]
    level_acc_ml[arch] = [
        (d[f"y_pred_{lvl}"] == d["y_test"][:, i]).mean() * 100
        for i, lvl in enumerate(LEVEL_NAMES)
    ]

# Load the single-level page's raw sub-class-only predictions, so its
# truncation-derived cascade can be plotted on the same axes for comparison.
PRED_BUCKET_SINGLE = "https://minio.lab.sspcloud.fr/projet-text-classif/predictions/naf"
ARCH_FILES_SINGLE  = {
    "FastText":                   "fasttext.npz",
    "FastText + Label Attention": "fasttext_labatt.npz",
}
PREDS_DIR_SINGLE = Path("results/naf/preds")
PREDS_DIR_SINGLE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

preds_by_arch_single = {}
for arch, fname in ARCH_FILES_SINGLE.items():
    cache = PREDS_DIR_SINGLE / fname
    try:
        if not cache.exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{PRED_BUCKET_SINGLE}/{fname}", cache)
        d = np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
        preds_by_arch_single[arch] = {
            "y_test": d["y_test"].astype(int), "y_pred": d["y_pred"].astype(int), "X_test": d["X_test"],
        }
    except Exception:
        pass

with open("assets/naf_labels.json") as f:
    NAF_LABEL_MAP_SINGLE = json.load(f)

def _single_class_code(idx):
    return NAF_LABEL_MAP_SINGLE.get(str(idx), "?")

DIVISION_TO_SECTION_SINGLE = {div: s["id"] for s in _naf_struct_ml["sections"] for div in s["divisions"]}

SINGLE_LEVELS = [
    ("Section",   lambda c: DIVISION_TO_SECTION_SINGLE.get(c[:2], "?")),
    ("Division",  lambda c: c[:2]),
    ("Group",     lambda c: c[:3]),
    ("Class",     lambda c: c[:4]),
    ("Sub-class", lambda c: c),
]

error_single = {}  # arch -> [error rate at sec, div, grp, cls, sub], from truncating the sub-class guess
for arch, d in preds_by_arch_single.items():
    true_codes = [_single_class_code(c) for c in d["y_test"]]
    pred_codes = [_single_class_code(c) for c in d["y_pred"]]
    error_single[arch] = [
        100 - np.mean([fn(t) == fn(p) for t, p in zip(true_codes, pred_codes)]) * 100
        for _, fn in SINGLE_LEVELS
    ]

x_lvls_ml = [LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in LEVEL_NAMES]

fig = go.Figure()
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML:
    err_ml = [100 - a for a in level_acc_ml[arch]]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x_lvls_ml, y=err_ml, mode="lines+markers", name=f"{arch} — multi-level heads",
        line=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(arch, "grey"), width=2.5), marker=dict(size=10),
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>error rate=%{y:.1f}%<extra>" + arch + " — multi-level</extra>",
    ))
for arch, errs in error_single.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x_lvls_ml, y=errs, mode="lines+markers", name=f"{arch} — single-level (truncated)",
        line=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(arch, "grey"), width=2.5, dash="dot"),
        marker=dict(size=8, symbol="diamond"),
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>error rate=%{y:.1f}%<extra>" + arch + " — single-level</extra>",
    ))

all_err_vals = [v for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML for v in [100 - a for a in level_acc_ml[arch]]]
all_err_vals += [v for errs in error_single.values() for v in errs]
y_pad = (max(all_err_vals) - min(all_err_vals)) * 0.1

fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white",
    xaxis_title="Hierarchy level", yaxis_title="Error rate (%)",
    yaxis=dict(range=[min(all_err_vals) - y_pad, max(all_err_vals) + y_pad]),
    legend_title="Architecture — approach", height=460,
)
fig.show()
```

The gap isn't monotonic in size, but it never reverses: truncating the single-level model's sub-class guess leads multi-level's own independent heads at every level, from over a point ahead at **Section** down to an exact tie at **Sub-class**, narrowing steadily through **Division**, **Group** and **Class** rather than crossing over. That convergence is worth flagging: single-level and multi-level are two *separately trained* models, not the same model with heads removed, so there's no reason to expect them to land this close even on the one task (sub-class) both nominally solve directly — whatever benefit the auxiliary per-level losses provide to multi-level's coarser heads, they don't appear to give its own sub-class head any edge over a model trained on that task alone.

The next view zooms into the wrong sub-class predictions only, and buckets each one by the *finest* of Class/Group/Division/Section that still lands correctly. For single-level, that bucket is unambiguous — truncation is nested by construction, so a correct division always implies a correct section too (section is deterministically derived from division), and conversely a wrong section forces division, group and class to be wrong as well. For multi-level, it's less obvious than it sounds: **"No match" means all four independent heads miss at once**, not just the section head — since the four heads are separately trained and never consult each other, it's entirely possible for the division head to land correctly while the (equally independent) section head misses the very same example, an inconsistency truncation can never produce.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hierarchy-errors-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Among wrong sub-class predictions, the finest level that still lands correctly — multi-level's independent heads vs. single-level's truncated cascade"

BUCKET_ORDER_ML = ["cls", "grp", "div", "sec"]
BUCKET_LABELS_ML = {"cls": "Class", "grp": "Group", "div": "Division", "sec": "Section"}
ERROR_BUCKETS_ML = ["Class", "Group", "Division", "Section", "No match"]
BUCKET_COLORS_ML = {
    "Class":      "#66BB6A",
    "Group":      "#FFCA28",
    "Division":   "#FB8C00",
    "Section":    "#E53935",
    "No match":   "#7B0000",
}

error_shares_ml = {}  # arch -> {bucket: pct of errors}
overall_acc_ml  = {}  # arch -> exact-match accuracy, for the x-axis subtitle
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML:
    d = preds_by_arch_ml[arch]
    y_test = d["y_test"]
    correct = {lvl: (d[f"y_pred_{lvl}"] == y_test[:, i]) for i, lvl in enumerate(LEVEL_NAMES)}
    overall_acc_ml[arch] = correct["sub"].mean() * 100

    wrong_idx = np.where(~correct["sub"])[0]
    assigned  = np.full(len(wrong_idx), "No match", dtype=object)
    remaining = np.ones(len(wrong_idx), dtype=bool)
    for lvl in BUCKET_ORDER_ML:
        is_correct_here = correct[lvl][wrong_idx] & remaining
        assigned[is_correct_here] = BUCKET_LABELS_ML[lvl]
        remaining &= ~is_correct_here

    counts = pd.Series(assigned).value_counts()
    error_shares_ml[arch] = {b: counts.get(b, 0) / len(wrong_idx) * 100 for b in ERROR_BUCKETS_ML}

# Same bucketing, applied to the single-level page's truncated cascade instead
# of independent heads, so both approaches can sit on the same chart.
SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY = {name: fn for name, fn in SINGLE_LEVELS}  # "Section"/"Division"/... -> fn
SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY = {
    "sec": SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY["Section"],
    "div": SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY["Division"],
    "grp": SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY["Group"],
    "cls": SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY["Class"],
}

error_shares_single = {}
overall_acc_single  = {}
for arch, d in preds_by_arch_single.items():
    true_codes  = np.array([_single_class_code(c) for c in d["y_test"]])
    pred_codes  = np.array([_single_class_code(c) for c in d["y_pred"]])
    correct_sub = true_codes == pred_codes
    overall_acc_single[arch] = correct_sub.mean() * 100

    wrong_idx = np.where(~correct_sub)[0]
    t_wrong, p_wrong = true_codes[wrong_idx], pred_codes[wrong_idx]
    assigned  = np.full(len(wrong_idx), "No match", dtype=object)
    remaining = np.ones(len(wrong_idx), dtype=bool)
    for lvl in BUCKET_ORDER_ML:
        fn = SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY[lvl]
        is_correct_here = (np.array([fn(t) for t in t_wrong]) == np.array([fn(p) for p in p_wrong])) & remaining
        assigned[is_correct_here] = BUCKET_LABELS_ML[lvl]
        remaining &= ~is_correct_here

    counts = pd.Series(assigned).value_counts()
    error_shares_single[arch] = {b: counts.get(b, 0) / len(wrong_idx) * 100 for b in ERROR_BUCKETS_ML}

bar_order = []  # [("ml"|"single", arch), ...] — same architecture's two bars kept adjacent
for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML:
    bar_order.append(("ml", arch))
    if arch in preds_by_arch_single:
        bar_order.append(("single", arch))

x_labels_combined = [
    f"{arch}<br>multi-level<i> ({100 - overall_acc_ml[arch]:.1f}% wrong)</i>" if kind == "ml"
    else f"{arch}<br>single-level<i> ({100 - overall_acc_single[arch]:.1f}% wrong)</i>"
    for kind, arch in bar_order
]
patterns_combined = ["" if kind == "ml" else "/" for kind, arch in bar_order]

fig = go.Figure()
for bucket in ERROR_BUCKETS_ML:
    vals = [
        error_shares_ml[arch][bucket] if kind == "ml" else error_shares_single[arch][bucket]
        for kind, arch in bar_order
    ]
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=x_labels_combined, y=vals, name=bucket,
        marker=dict(color=BUCKET_COLORS_ML[bucket], pattern=dict(shape=patterns_combined)),
        text=[f"{v:.1f}%" for v in vals],
        textposition="inside", insidetextfont=dict(color="white", size=11),
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>" + bucket + ": %{y:.1f}% of errors<extra></extra>",
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white", barmode="stack",
    xaxis_title=None, yaxis_title="Share of wrong sub-class predictions (%)",
    yaxis=dict(range=[0, 100]),
    legend_title="Finest level<br>that still lands right", height=480,
)
fig.show()
```

The single-level bars (hatched) confirm this isn't just an artefact of the earlier derived comparison: on [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd), ≈47–48% of errors are "No match" (not even the section is right) for both architectures, and only ≈7–8% stay within the correct class. Multi-level's independent heads do much better on both counts: "No match" is only **34.0%** for FastText and **28.9%** for Label Attention, and — unlike the single-level bars, which look nearly identical to each other — the two architectures now diverge meaningfully, with Label Attention landing in the **Class** bucket far more often (25.1% vs. 11.3% for FastText). When its finest guess is wrong, its independently-trained class head is much more likely to still be right, even though its raw sub-class accuracy is slightly lower. The auxiliary heads are doing real work that the single-level bars, sitting right next to them, simply cannot do.

### Effect of independent heads

The buckets in the previous tab already prove the auxiliary heads are doing real work, but they still read like an abstract accounting exercise. This tab isolates the mechanism directly — the single-level model is not involved here, both sides of the comparison come from the **multi-level model alone**: restricted to the exact same wrong-sub-class examples, how often does *truncating* that same model's own wrong sub-class guess land on the truth, versus how often does its *independent* head get it right on its own?

```{python}
#| label: fig-hierarchy-independence-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Section/division accuracy among wrong sub-class predictions: truncating the wrong guess vs. asking the independent head directly"

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

GAP_LEVELS_ML  = ["sec", "div"]
GAP_LABELS_ML  = {"sec": "Section", "div": "Division"}

DIVISION_TO_SECTION_ML = {div: s["id"] for s in _naf_struct_ml["sections"] for div in s["divisions"]}

def code_section_gap(code):
    return DIVISION_TO_SECTION_ML.get(code[:2], "?")

def code_division_gap(code):
    return code[:2]
TRUNC_FNS_ML = {"sec": code_section_gap, "div": code_division_gap}

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=len(ARCHS_AVAIL_ML), subplot_titles=ARCHS_AVAIL_ML,
                    horizontal_spacing=0.12)

for col, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_AVAIL_ML, start=1):
    d = preds_by_arch_ml[arch]
    y_test = d["y_test"]
    wrong_sub = d["y_pred_sub"] != y_test[:, 4]
    pred_sub_codes = np.array([code_of("sub", c) for c in d["y_pred_sub"][wrong_sub]])

    trunc_accs, direct_accs = [], []
    for i, lvl in enumerate(GAP_LEVELS_ML):
        true_codes  = np.array([code_of(lvl, c) for c in y_test[wrong_sub, i]])
        trunc_codes = np.array([TRUNC_FNS_ML[lvl](c) for c in pred_sub_codes])
        trunc_accs.append((trunc_codes == true_codes).mean() * 100)
        direct_accs.append((d[f"y_pred_{lvl}"][wrong_sub] == y_test[wrong_sub, i]).mean() * 100)

    x_labels = [GAP_LABELS_ML[l] for l in GAP_LEVELS_ML]
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=x_labels, y=trunc_accs, name="Truncated (from the wrong sub-class guess)",
        legendgroup="trunc", showlegend=(col == 1),
        marker=dict(color="#bbbbbb", pattern_shape="/"),
        text=[f"{v:.1f}%" for v in trunc_accs], textposition="outside",
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>truncated: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>",
    ), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=x_labels, y=direct_accs, name="Direct (independent head)",
        legendgroup="direct", showlegend=(col == 1),
        marker=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(arch, "grey")),
        text=[f"{v:.1f}%" for v in direct_accs], textposition="outside",
        hovertemplate="%{x}<br>direct: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>",
    ), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 75], title_text="Accuracy (%)" if col == 1 else "", row=1, col=col)

fig.update_layout(
    barmode="group", template="simple_white", height=440,
    legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=-0.18, yanchor="top"),
    margin=dict(t=40, b=80),
)
fig.show()
```

For both architectures and both levels, the grey (truncated) bar is consistently well below the coloured (direct) bar — the independent head recovers real accuracy that a truncation-only view throws away: +8.6pp at section / +9.6pp at division for FastText, +9.9pp / +13.1pp for Label Attention. This is the concrete mechanism behind the previous tab's better "No match" rate: it isn't that the model becomes more accurate overall, it's that its mistakes are genuinely *localised to one head* — the sub-class head can misfire on the fine-grained decision while the division and section heads, trained with their own independent loss on the same shared token encoding, are unaffected and still answer correctly.

**Why not group and class too?** 576 of the 651 NAF classes (88.5%) contain exactly **one** sub-class — for those, getting the class right and getting the sub-class right are the same event, so whenever the sub-class head is wrong, truncating that wrong guess to class level is *necessarily* also wrong: truncated accuracy collapses to ~0% at those two levels, which would make the comparison trivial rather than informative. Section and division are coarse enough that many different sub-classes map to the same coarser code, so truncation and direct prediction can genuinely diverge — that's what the chart above needs to be meaningful.

### Top section confusions

```{python}
#| label: fig-topflows-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Top misclassification flows between NAF sections (true section → predicted section), predicted directly"

N_FLOWS_ML = 15

def _top_flows_ml(arch):
    d = preds_by_arch_ml[arch]
    true_sec = [code_of("sec", c) for c in d["y_test"][:, 0]]
    pred_sec = [code_of("sec", c) for c in d["y_pred_sec"]]
    flow_counts = defaultdict(int)
    for t, p in zip(true_sec, pred_sec):
        if t != p:
            flow_counts[(t, p)] += 1
    top = sorted(flow_counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:N_FLOWS_ML]
    return top[::-1]  # reversed: largest ends up at the top of the horizontal bar

n_archs_ml = len(ARCHS_AVAIL_ML)
fig = go.Figure()

for i, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_AVAIL_ML):
    top = _top_flows_ml(arch)
    labels = [f"{t} → {p}" for (t, p), _ in top]
    counts = [cnt for _, cnt in top]
    colors = [SECTION_COLOR_ML.get(t, "#888888") for (t, p), _ in top]
    hover  = [f"{SECTION_LABEL_ML.get(t, t)} → {SECTION_LABEL_ML.get(p, p)}" for (t, p), _ in top]
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=counts, y=labels, orientation="h",
        marker=dict(color=colors),
        customdata=hover,
        text=[str(c) for c in counts], textposition="outside",
        hovertemplate="<b>%{customdata}</b><br>%{x} misclassifications<extra></extra>",
        visible=(i == 0),
    ))

buttons = [dict(
    label=arch, method="update",
    args=[{"visible": [j == i for j in range(n_archs_ml)]}],
) for i, arch in enumerate(ARCHS_AVAIL_ML)]

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Number of misclassifications (true → predicted section)",
    yaxis_title=None,
    height=550, margin=dict(l=10, r=40, t=60, b=40),
    updatemenus=[dict(
        type="dropdown", buttons=buttons,
        x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=1.08, yanchor="top",
        showactive=True, bgcolor="#f0f0f0", bordercolor="#ccc",
        font=dict(size=12),
    )],
)
fig.show()
```

The two largest flows both involve section **M** (scientific & technical activities) — confused with **K** (financial & insurance, 7.0% of FastText's section-level errors) and **J** (information & communication, 6.2%), with the reverse flow J→M also in the top three (6.2%). This is a symmetric, semantically coherent confusion: consulting, IT, and technical-services activities genuinely overlap in vocabulary with finance and information-services activities, and it shows up as a real bidirectional flow rather than a one-way drain into a single dominant class — unlike the OOS "catch-all" pattern seen on CLINC150.

### Examples

```{python}
#| label: fig-examples-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Example predictions across all five hierarchy levels"

import random
random.seed(42)

y_test_all_ml = preds_by_arch_ml[ARCHS_AVAIL_ML[0]]["y_test"]  # (50000, 5)

df_ex_ml = pd.DataFrame({"text": X_TEST_ML})
for i, lvl in enumerate(LEVEL_NAMES):
    df_ex_ml[f"true_{lvl}"] = y_test_all_ml[:, i]
    for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML:
        df_ex_ml[f"{arch}__{lvl}"] = preds_by_arch_ml[arch][f"y_pred_{lvl}"]

sub_cols_ml = [f"{arch}__sub" for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML]
df_ex_ml["disagree"]  = df_ex_ml[sub_cols_ml].nunique(axis=1) > 1
df_ex_ml["any_wrong"] = (df_ex_ml[sub_cols_ml].values != df_ex_ml[["true_sub"]].values).any(axis=1)
pool_ml   = df_ex_ml[df_ex_ml["disagree"] & df_ex_ml["any_wrong"]]
sample_ml = pool_ml.sample(min(12, len(pool_ml)), random_state=42).reset_index(drop=True)

def fmt_ml(level, idx):
    code = code_of(level, int(idx))
    lbl  = label_of(level, code)
    return f"{code} — {lbl}" if lbl != code else code

def fmt_code_ml(level, code):
    lbl = label_of(level, code)
    return f"{code} — {lbl}" if lbl != code else code

def truncate_code_ml(level, code):
    return code if level == "sub" else SINGLE_LEVEL_FN_BY_KEY[level](code)

# Text -> row lookup into the single-level page's own (separately trained)
# test set, so each sampled utterance can be matched to its single-level
# prediction too — verified to fully overlap (all 50k multi-level test texts
# are also present in single-level's 50k test set, same cleaning pipeline).
single_lookup_ml = {
    arch: {str(t): i for i, t in enumerate(d["X_test"])}
    for arch, d in preds_by_arch_single.items()
}

examples_ml = []
for _, r in sample_ml.iterrows():
    text = str(r["text"])
    preds_entry = {}
    for arch in ARCHS_AVAIL_ML:
        sub_code_own = code_of("sub", int(r[f"{arch}__sub"]))
        preds_entry[arch] = {
            "direct":     {lvl: fmt_ml(lvl, r[f"{arch}__{lvl}"]) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES},
            "trunc_own":  {lvl: fmt_code_ml(lvl, truncate_code_ml(lvl, sub_code_own)) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES},
            "trunc_single": None,
        }
        idx_single = single_lookup_ml.get(arch, {}).get(text)
        if idx_single is not None:
            sub_code_single = _single_class_code(int(preds_by_arch_single[arch]["y_pred"][idx_single]))
            preds_entry[arch]["trunc_single"] = {
                lvl: fmt_code_ml(lvl, truncate_code_ml(lvl, sub_code_single)) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES
            }

    examples_ml.append({
        "text": text,
        "true": {lvl: fmt_ml(lvl, r[f"true_{lvl}"]) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES},
        "preds": preds_entry,
    })

html = f"""
<style>

  .exml-card   {{ border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:8px; padding:20px 24px;
                  background:#fafafa; margin-bottom:14px; }}

  .exml-nav    {{ display:flex; align-items:center; gap:12px; justify-content:center; margin-bottom:12px; }}
```
