```{python}
                  border-radius:5px; cursor:pointer; font-size:13px; }}
  .exml-btn:hover {{ background:#e0e0e0; }}
  .exml-count  {{ font-size:12px; color:#999; }}
</style>

<div class="exml-wrap">
  <div class="exml-nav">
    <button class="exml-btn" onclick="exNafMlNav(-1)">← Prev</button>
    <span class="exml-count" id="exml-count"></span>
    <button class="exml-btn" onclick="exNafMlNav(1)">Next →</button>
  </div>
  <div class="exml-card">
    <div class="exml-text" id="exml-text"></div>
    <div id="exml-table-wrap"></div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
(function() {{
  const EX = {json.dumps(examples_ml)};
  const LEVELS = {json.dumps(LEVEL_NAMES)};
  const LEVEL_LABELS = {json.dumps(LEVEL_LABELS_ML)};
  const ARCHS = {json.dumps(ARCHS_AVAIL_ML)};
  const ARCH_SHORT = {json.dumps({"FastText": "FT", "FastText + Label Attention": "FT+LabAtt"})};
  let cur = 0;

  function render(i) {{
    const e = EX[i];
    document.getElementById('exml-text').textContent = '"' + e.text + '"';

    // Built as one HTML string and injected into a plain <div> rather than
    // pre-declaring an empty <table>/<thead>: Quarto's HTML post-processing
    // (Pandoc) reinterprets raw <table> elements and drops an empty <thead>
    // at build time (before this JS ever runs), silently breaking the ids
    // it depends on. A plain div is passed through untouched.
    // Transposed layout — one row per (architecture, variant), one column per
    // hierarchy level — so the table stays narrow instead of needing 8 columns.
    let head = '<th>Prediction</th>';
    for (const lvl of LEVELS) head += '<th>' + LEVEL_LABELS[lvl] + '</th>';
    head = '<tr>' + head + '</tr>';

    let rows = '<tr><td class="exml-lvl">True</td>';
    for (const lvl of LEVELS) rows += '<td>' + e.true[lvl] + '</td>';
    rows += '</tr>';

    for (const arch of ARCHS) {{
      const p = e.preds[arch];
      const archShort = ARCH_SHORT[arch] || arch;
      const variantDefs = [['Indep. heads', p.direct], ['Trunc. (multi)', p.trunc_own], ['Trunc. (single)', p.trunc_single]];
      for (const [label, data] of variantDefs) {{
        rows += '<tr><td class="exml-lvl">' + archShort + ' — ' + label + '</td>';
        for (const lvl of LEVELS) {{
          if (!data) {{
            rows += '<td style="color:#aaa;">n/a</td>';
          }} else {{
            const val = data[lvl];
            const cls = val === e.true[lvl] ? 'exml-correct' : 'exml-wrong';
            rows += '<td><span class="' + cls + '">' + val + '</span></td>';
          }}
        }}
        rows += '</tr>';
      }}
    }}
    document.getElementById('exml-table-wrap').innerHTML =
      '<table class="exml-table"><thead>' + head + '</thead><tbody>' + rows + '</tbody></table>';
    document.getElementById('exml-count').textContent = (i + 1) + ' / ' + EX.length;
  }}

  window.exNafMlNav = function(d) {{ cur = (cur + d + EX.length) % EX.length; render(cur); }};
  render(0);
}})();
</script>
"""
HTML(html)
```

Browsing through these cards turns up the independent-heads quirk from the top of the page in concrete form: it's not rare to see the **sub-class** head land exactly right while the (independently predicted) **section** head misses — a combination truncation could never produce, since a correct sub-class would truncate down to a correct section every time. Here, the two heads simply disagree, each having made its own call from the shared encoding.

:::

## Explainability

This section asks *why* the multi-level model predicts what it predicts — and, unlike [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd), it can ask that question **five times over**, once per independent head. The same description now gets five separate explanations (section, division, group, class, sub-class), which opens a question single-level explainability can't: does the model rely on different words to justify a coarse call than a fine one? And when a "smart mistake" happens — right section, wrong sub-class, as seen throughout the Prediction analysis section above — what did each head actually look at?

The comparison is again between **FastText** and **FastText + Label Attention**, each level's own independently-trained head, on the same 200 sampled test descriptions.

Three complementary instruments, same as on the single-level page:

- **Layer Integrated Gradients (Captum)**: word-level attribution, computed independently for each of the 5 heads. Run without any class cap here — the cap used for label attention below wasn't needed for Captum, whose arrays carry no per-head dimension.
- **Label-attention weights** (Label Attention model only): the model's own cross-attention, also computed per level. Unlike Captum, this one *does* carry an extra head dimension (4 attention heads per level's mechanism) on top of the class dimension — summed across 5 levels' worth of ~1700 classes, the raw version was too large to log reliably, so it's capped to each level's top-100 predicted classes (no cap actually bites at section or division, which have fewer than 100 classes to begin with).
- **Class direction vectors**: per level, the label-attention queries or the linear head's weight rows — five geometries to compare instead of one.

```{python}
#| label: load-explain-artifacts-naf-multilevel

EXPLAIN_BUCKET_ML  = "https://minio.lab.sspcloud.fr/projet-text-classif/explanations/naf_multilevel"
_ARTIFACT_NAMES_ML = ["captum.npz", "label_attn.npz", "class_vectors.npz", "faithfulness.npz"]
_NOT_APPLICABLE_ML = {("pooling", "label_attn.npz")}  # mean pooling has no label attention mechanism

def _load_artifact_explain_ml(method: str, name: str):
    """Fetch (and cache) one multi-level explainability artifact; None if unavailable."""
    if (method, name) in _NOT_APPLICABLE_ML:
        return None
    cache_dir = Path("results/naf_multilevel/explain") / method
    cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cache = cache_dir / name
    try:
        if not cache.exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{EXPLAIN_BUCKET_ML}/{method}/{name}", cache)
        return np.load(cache, allow_pickle=True)
    except Exception:
        return None

cap_la_ml, lat_la_ml, cv_la_ml, fai_la_ml = (_load_artifact_explain_ml("labatt",  n) for n in _ARTIFACT_NAMES_ML)
cap_pl_ml, lat_pl_ml, cv_pl_ml, fai_pl_ml = (_load_artifact_explain_ml("pooling", n) for n in _ARTIFACT_NAMES_ML)

HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML = cap_la_ml is not None

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    print("Explainability artifacts not yet available — re-run src/multilevel/explain.py")
else:
    EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML = {"labatt": "FastText + Label Attention", "pooling": "FastText"}
    EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML     = {"labatt": cap_la_ml, "pooling": cap_pl_ml}
    EXPLAIN_LABEL_ATTN_ML = {"labatt": lat_la_ml, "pooling": lat_pl_ml}
    EXPLAIN_CLASS_VECS_ML = {"labatt": cv_la_ml,  "pooling": cv_pl_ml}
    EXPLAIN_FAITHFUL_ML   = {"labatt": fai_la_ml, "pooling": fai_pl_ml}
    EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML = [k for k in ("labatt", "pooling") if EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML[k] is not None]
```

### Word attributions across the hierarchy

*Method: Captum (Integrated Gradients)*

For a single description, each level's head reaches its own verdict from the same shared encoding — the figure below renders all five as **highlighted text**, stacked, using that level's own attribution for whatever class it actually predicted. Green pushes toward that level's prediction, red pushes away, colour intensity ∝ `|score| / max|score|` within that row.

The examples below are deliberately picked to include the "smart mistakes" quantified earlier in Prediction analysis — right section, wrong sub-class — alongside a couple of clean sweeps (every level correct) and clean misses (every level wrong), so the shift in emphasis from coarse to fine rows is easy to compare.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-hierarchy-highlight-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Captum attributions for the predicted class at each hierarchy level, same description throughout. Use the ← / → arrows to switch examples."

import json
from IPython.display import HTML, display

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    out_ml = HTML("<p>Artifacts not yet available.</p>")
else:
    def _cls_display_ml(level: str, idx: int) -> str:
        code = code_of(level, idx)
        lbl  = label_of(level, code)
        return f"{code} — {lbl}" if lbl != code else code

    rng_ml = np.random.default_rng(7)
    picks_ml = []  # (arch, example_idx)
    for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML:
        cap = EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML[arch]
        correct_sec = cap["y_pred_sec"] == cap["y_true_sec"]
        correct_sub = cap["y_pred_sub"] == cap["y_true_sub"]
        seen  = {i for _, i in picks_ml}
        smart = [i for i in np.where(correct_sec & ~correct_sub)[0] if i not in seen]
        rng_ml.shuffle(smart)
        picks_ml += [(arch, int(i)) for i in smart[:3]]
        seen    = {i for _, i in picks_ml}
        both_ok = [i for i in np.where(correct_sec & correct_sub)[0] if i not in seen]
        rng_ml.shuffle(both_ok)
        picks_ml += [(arch, int(i)) for i in both_ok[:2]]
        seen       = {i for _, i in picks_ml}
        both_wrong = [i for i in np.where(~correct_sec & ~correct_sub)[0] if i not in seen]
        rng_ml.shuffle(both_wrong)
        picks_ml += [(arch, int(i)) for i in both_wrong[:2]]

    def _spans_html_ml(words, scores):
        amax = max((abs(s) for s in scores), default=1) or 1
        parts = []
        for j, w in enumerate(words):
            s = scores[j] if j < len(scores) else 0
            t = abs(s) / amax
            rgb = "57,255,20" if s >= 0 else "255,30,30"
            alpha = round(0.10 + 0.65 * t, 2)
            parts.append(
                f'<span style="background-color:rgba({rgb},{alpha});'
                f'padding:1px 3px;margin:0 1px;line-height:2.3;">{w}</span>'
            )
        return " ".join(parts)

    cards_ml = []
    for arch, i in picks_ml:
        cap  = EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML[arch]
        text = str(cap["texts"][i])[:200]
        rows_html = ""
        for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES:
            words = [str(w) for w in list(cap[f"words_{lvl}"][i])[:40]]
            mat   = cap[f"word_attn_{lvl}"][i]  # (n_classes, n_words), row 0 = predicted class
            pred  = int(cap[f"y_pred_{lvl}"][i])
            true  = int(cap[f"y_true_{lvl}"][i])
            ok    = pred == true
            nw    = min(len(words), mat.shape[1])
            bc    = "#2E7D32" if ok else "#B71C1C"
            mark  = "✓" if ok else "✗"
            rows_html += (
                f'<div style="margin:8px 0;">'
                f'<div style="font-size:11.5px;color:#777;margin-bottom:2px;">'
                f'<b style="color:#333;">{LEVEL_LABELS_ML[lvl]}</b> → '
                f'{_cls_display_ml(lvl, pred)} <span style="color:{bc};">{mark}</span></div>'
                f'<div style="line-height:2.4;">{_spans_html_ml(words[:nw], mat[0][:nw])}</div>'
                f'</div>'
            )
        cards_ml.append(
            f'<div style="border:1px solid #e2e2e2;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;background:#fcfcfc;">'
            f'<div style="font-size:13px;color:#444;margin-bottom:10px;">'
            f'<b>{EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch]}</b> &mdash; <i>&ldquo;{text}&rdquo;</i></div>'
            f'{rows_html}</div>'
        )

    nav_id_ml  = "hl-nav-ml"
    n_cards_ml = len(cards_ml)
    hl_html_ml = f"""
<div style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:14px;">
  <div style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:12px;justify-content:center;margin-bottom:12px;">
    <button style="padding:6px 18px;background:#f0f0f0;border:1px solid #ccc;border-radius:5px;cursor:pointer;font-size:13px;"
            onclick="hlNavMl(-1)">← Prev</button>
    <span id="{nav_id_ml}-cnt" style="font-size:12px;color:#999;">1 / {n_cards_ml}</span>
    <button style="padding:6px 18px;background:#f0f0f0;border:1px solid #ccc;border-radius:5px;cursor:pointer;font-size:13px;"
            onclick="hlNavMl(1)">Next →</button>
  </div>
  <div id="{nav_id_ml}">{cards_ml[0] if cards_ml else ""}</div>
</div>
<script>
(function() {{
  window._hlCardsMl = {json.dumps(cards_ml)};
  window._hlCurMl   = 0;
  window.hlNavMl = function(d) {{
    window._hlCurMl = (window._hlCurMl + d + window._hlCardsMl.length) % window._hlCardsMl.length;
    document.getElementById('{nav_id_ml}').innerHTML = window._hlCardsMl[window._hlCurMl];
    document.getElementById('{nav_id_ml}-cnt').textContent = (window._hlCurMl + 1) + ' / ' + window._hlCardsMl.length;
  }};
}})();
</script>
"""
    out_ml = HTML(hl_html_ml)

display(out_ml)
```

### Label attention across the hierarchy

*Method: label-attention weights*

Captum is a post-hoc reconstruction; label attention is the model's *own* explanation, built into the architecture — each level's head literally attends to specific words before deciding. For one description, here is that raw attention (averaged over the mechanism's 4 heads), one heatmap per level, restricted to the 10 classes each head found most plausible (plus the true class, if it happens to fall outside that top 10). Rows are sub-classes-of-that-level, columns are the description's words.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-labatt-hierarchy-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Label attention (mean over heads) for one example, at each hierarchy level — top 10 predicted classes, plus the true class if not already among them."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML or lat_la_ml is None:
    print("Label attention artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    _TOP_K_LAH_ML = 10

    cap0 = EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML["labatt"]
    _correct_sec0 = cap0["y_pred_sec"] == cap0["y_true_sec"]
    _correct_sub0 = cap0["y_pred_sub"] == cap0["y_true_sub"]
    _smart0 = np.where(_correct_sec0 & ~_correct_sub0)[0]
    ex_idx_lah_ml = int(_smart0[0]) if len(_smart0) else 0

    fig = make_subplots(
        rows=1, cols=len(LEVEL_NAMES),
        subplot_titles=[LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in LEVEL_NAMES],
        horizontal_spacing=0.04,
    )
    for col, lvl in enumerate(LEVEL_NAMES, start=1):
        words       = [str(w) for w in lat_la_ml[f"words_{lvl}"][ex_idx_lah_ml]]
        head_word   = lat_la_ml[f"head_word_attn_{lvl}"][ex_idx_lah_ml]  # (n_head, k_kept, n_words)
        class_order = lat_la_ml[f"class_order_{lvl}"][ex_idx_lah_ml]    # (k_kept,) actual class idx, confidence order
        true_cls    = int(lat_la_ml[f"y_true_{lvl}"][ex_idx_lah_ml])

        sel = list(class_order[:_TOP_K_LAH_ML])
        if true_cls not in sel and true_cls in class_order:
            sel = sel[:-1] + [true_cls]
        idx_map  = {int(c): k for k, c in enumerate(class_order)}
        rows_sel = [idx_map[c] for c in sel]

        mean_attn = head_word.mean(axis=0)  # (k_kept, n_words)
        z = mean_attn[rows_sel]
        y_labels = [code_of(lvl, c) for c in sel]

        fig.add_trace(go.Heatmap(
            z=z, x=words, y=y_labels, coloraxis="coloraxis",
            hovertemplate="word=%{x}<br>class=%{y}<br>weight=%{z:.3f}<extra></extra>",
        ), row=1, col=col)

    fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False)
    fig.update_layout(
        height=380, coloraxis=dict(colorscale="Viridis"),
        margin=dict(t=60, b=20, l=20, r=20),
        paper_bgcolor="white",
    )
    fig.show()
```

Averaged over all 200 examples, the mean-over-heads attention shows the same pattern already seen for Captum: no clear coarse-to-fine trend in *how* concentrated it gets (a fairly flat 38–40% resting in the single most-attended word at every level). What visibly changes between the five panels above, for this one example, is *which* words and classes draw that attention, not how sharply it's split among them — the mechanism-level counterpart to the word-attribution shift shown just above.

### Corpus-level word importance, direct at the section level

*Method: Captum (Integrated Gradients)*

On [Single-level classification](naf_single.qmd), the equivalent figure had to *approximate* section-level importance by grouping together the attributions of whichever sub-classes happen to fall under each section — there was no section-level prediction to ask directly. Here there is: the section head is independently trained, so the word importance below comes straight from it, for the 6 best-represented sections in the test sample.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-corpus-sec-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Top attributed words for the 6 best-represented NAF sections, using the section head's own direct predictions."

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    def _section_top_ml(cap, sec_code, top_n=8):
        idx = np.where(np.array([code_of("sec", c) for c in cap["y_pred_sec"]]) == sec_code)[0]
        scores, counts = {}, {}
        for i in idx:
            words = [str(w) for w in cap["words_sec"][i]]
            attn  = np.abs(cap["word_attn_sec"][i][0][:len(words)])
            for w, s in zip(words, attn):
                w_l = w.lower()
                scores[w_l] = scores.get(w_l, 0.0) + float(s)
                counts[w_l] = counts.get(w_l, 0) + 1
        if not scores:
            return []
        ranked = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1] / counts[kv[0]])
        return [(w, s / counts[w]) for w, s in ranked[:top_n]]

    _key_corpus_ml = "labatt" if "labatt" in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML else EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML[0]
    cap_corpus_ml  = EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML[_key_corpus_ml]

    sec_counts_ml       = pd.Series([code_of("sec", c) for c in cap_corpus_ml["y_true_sec"]]).value_counts()
    N_SECTIONS_SHOWN_ML = 6
    shown_sections_ml   = sec_counts_ml.index[:N_SECTIONS_SHOWN_ML].tolist()

    ROWS_ML, COLS_ML = 2, 3
    titles_ml = [f"{s} — {SECTION_LABEL_ML[s].replace('Activités', 'Act.')}" for s in shown_sections_ml]
    fig = make_subplots(rows=ROWS_ML, cols=COLS_ML, subplot_titles=titles_ml,
                         horizontal_spacing=0.09, vertical_spacing=0.20)

    for si, sec in enumerate(shown_sections_ml):
        row, col = si // COLS_ML + 1, si % COLS_ML + 1
        top = _section_top_ml(cap_corpus_ml, sec)[::-1]
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
            x=[s for _, s in top], y=[w for w, _ in top], orientation="h",
            marker=dict(color=SECTION_COLOR_ML.get(sec, "#888888"), line=dict(width=0)),
            width=0.6, opacity=0.9, showlegend=False,
            hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>Mean |IG|: %{x:.4f}<extra></extra>",
        ), row=row, col=col)

    for i, ann in enumerate(fig.layout.annotations):
        if i < len(shown_sections_ml):
            ann.font.size = 13
            ann.font.color = SECTION_COLOR_ML.get(shown_sections_ml[i], "#333")

    fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor="#f0f0f0", tickfont=dict(size=10))
    fig.update_yaxes(tickfont=dict(size=11), showgrid=False)
    fig.update_layout(height=620, margin=dict(t=70, b=30, l=20, r=20), paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white")
    fig.show()
```

### How concentrated are these explanations?

*Method: Captum (Integrated Gradients)*

A different question from *which* words matter: *how many* of them does the model actually lean on? For each description, we take its predicted class's attribution row and measure what share of the total `|attribution|` mass sits in the single most-attributed word — averaged across examples, per level.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-concentration-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Mean share of a description's total |attribution| mass carried by its single most-attributed word, for the predicted class, by hierarchy level."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    def _top_word_share_ml(cap, lvl):
        shares = []
        for i in range(len(cap[f"word_attn_{lvl}"])):
            row   = np.abs(cap[f"word_attn_{lvl}"][i][0])
            total = row.sum()
            if total > 0:
                shares.append(row.max() / total)
        return float(np.mean(shares)) * 100

    concentration_ml = {
        arch: [_top_word_share_ml(EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML[arch], lvl) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES]
        for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML
    }

    fig = go.Figure()
    for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=[LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in LEVEL_NAMES], y=concentration_ml[arch],
            mode="lines+markers", name=EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch],
            line=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch], "grey"), width=2.5),
            marker=dict(size=9),
        ))
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="Hierarchy level", yaxis_title="Mean top-word share of |attribution| (%)",
        legend_title="Architecture", height=420, yaxis=dict(range=[30, 50]),
    )
    fig.show()
```

Label Attention's explanations are consistently more concentrated in a single word than FastText's — roughly 3 to 6 points higher at every level (≈41–45% vs. ≈37–40%) — but neither architecture shows a clear coarse-to-fine trend: both hover in a narrow band regardless of whether the head is making a 20-way section call or a 679-way sub-class call. The gap is between architectures, not between levels: label attention's per-class query vectors appear to latch onto a narrower keyword signature than mean pooling's more diffuse bag-of-embeddings attribution, at every granularity.

### Are these explanations faithful across the hierarchy?

*Method: Captum (Integrated Gradients), word-deletion stress test*

The same faithfulness test used on the single-level page — delete the words Captum ranked as most important and watch the predicted class's probability collapse, against a random-removal control — run independently at each level. First, the raw curves themselves, one small panel per level; then the **gap** between the two curves (area between random and guided) as a single headline number per level: bigger means Captum's ranking is a more trustworthy guide to what that level's head actually uses.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-faithfulness-curves-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Faithfulness (comprehensiveness) test at each hierarchy level: mean probability retained by the predicted class as the most-attributed words are progressively deleted (solid = guided removal by |Captum score|; dotted = random-removal control). Shaded bands show ±1 std across examples."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    RGB_ML = {"FastText": "33,150,243", "FastText + Label Attention": "0,188,212"}

    ROWS_FAI_ML, COLS_FAI_ML = 2, 3
    fig = make_subplots(
        rows=ROWS_FAI_ML, cols=COLS_FAI_ML,
        subplot_titles=[LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in LEVEL_NAMES],
        horizontal_spacing=0.06, vertical_spacing=0.16,
    )

    for li, lvl in enumerate(LEVEL_NAMES):
        row, col = li // COLS_FAI_ML + 1, li % COLS_FAI_ML + 1
        for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML:
            fai   = EXPLAIN_FAITHFUL_ML[arch]
            fr    = fai[f"fractions_{lvl}"]
            label = EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch]
            color = COLORS_ML.get(label, "grey")
            rgb   = RGB_ML.get(label, "120,120,120")
            for arr, dash in [(fai[f"guided_probs_{lvl}"], "solid"), (fai[f"random_probs_{lvl}"], "dot")]:
                m, s = np.nanmean(arr, axis=0), np.nanstd(arr, axis=0)
                fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                    x=np.concatenate([fr, fr[::-1]]), y=np.concatenate([m + s, (m - s)[::-1]]),
                    fill="toself", fillcolor=f"rgba({rgb},0.10)", line=dict(width=0),
                    mode="lines", showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip",
                ), row=row, col=col)
                fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                    x=fr, y=m, mode="lines", line=dict(color=color, dash=dash, width=2),
                    name=label, legendgroup=label,
                    showlegend=(li == 0 and dash == "solid"),
                    hovertemplate="fraction removed=%{x}<br>retained prob.=%{y:.3f}<extra>" + label + "</extra>",
                ), row=row, col=col)
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 1.02], row=row, col=col)

    fig.update_layout(
        height=560, margin=dict(t=60, b=20, l=20, r=20),
        paper_bgcolor="white", plot_bgcolor="white",
    )
    fig.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-faithfulness-hierarchy-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Faithfulness gap (area between random- and guided-removal curves) by hierarchy level."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    def _faithfulness_gap_ml(fai, lvl):
        g = np.nanmean(fai[f"guided_probs_{lvl}"], axis=0)
        r = np.nanmean(fai[f"random_probs_{lvl}"], axis=0)
        return float(np.trapezoid(r - g, fai[f"fractions_{lvl}"]))

    gaps_ml = {
        arch: [_faithfulness_gap_ml(EXPLAIN_FAITHFUL_ML[arch], lvl) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES]
        for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML
    }

    fig = go.Figure()
    for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=[LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in LEVEL_NAMES], y=gaps_ml[arch],
            mode="lines+markers", name=EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch],
            line=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch], "grey"), width=2.5),
            marker=dict(size=9),
        ))
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="Hierarchy level", yaxis_title="Faithfulness gap (random − guided)",
        legend_title="Architecture", height=420,
    )
    fig.show()
```

FastText's Captum ranking is the more trustworthy guide overall, by a wide and stable margin: its gap sits at ≈0.31 at every level except section (≈0.25), meaning its top-ranked words collapse the predicted class roughly 3× faster than random removal, regardless of hierarchy depth. Label Attention's gap is smaller everywhere — its post-hoc Captum explanation is a noticeably less reliable guide to what it actually uses — and, unlike FastText, it drifts upward from coarse to fine (0.045 at group → 0.133 at class → 0.171 at sub-class), though section (0.076) breaks strict monotonicity by sitting above group. Label attention's explanations only approach FastText's level of faithfulness at the finest sub-class head — consistent with the sharper-but-less-validated attributions seen just above.

### Class geometry across the hierarchy

*Method: class direction vectors*

Does the classification space get more crowded as the hierarchy narrows? For each level, we take that level's class vectors (label-attention query vectors for Label Attention, linear classification-head weight rows for FastText) and compute the mean pairwise cosine similarity between classes — higher means classes sit closer together in that space.

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-geometry-hierarchy-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Mean pairwise cosine similarity between class direction vectors, by hierarchy level."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    def _mean_cos_sim_ml(vecs, sample=2000, seed=0):
        v = vecs / (np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)
        n = v.shape[0]
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        if n > sample:
            idx = rng.choice(n, size=sample, replace=False)
            v = v[idx]
        sim = v @ v.T
        iu = np.triu_indices(v.shape[0], k=1)
        return float(sim[iu].mean())

    geometry_ml = {
        arch: [
            _mean_cos_sim_ml(EXPLAIN_CLASS_VECS_ML[arch][f"class_vectors_{lvl}"])
            for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES
        ]
        for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML
    }

    fig = go.Figure()
    for arch in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=[LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in LEVEL_NAMES], y=geometry_ml[arch],
            mode="lines+markers", name=EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch],
            line=dict(color=COLORS_ML.get(EXPLAIN_MODEL_LABELS_ML[arch], "grey"), width=2.5),
            marker=dict(size=9),
        ))
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="Hierarchy level", yaxis_title="Mean pairwise cosine similarity",
        legend_title="Architecture", height=420,
    )
    fig.show()
```

FastText's classification-head geometry crowds together steadily as the hierarchy narrows: classes go from nearly orthogonal at section (mean cosine ≈ −0.02, 20 classes) to noticeably closer at sub-class (≈0.18, 679 classes) — roughly what you'd expect from packing more categories into the same embedding space. Label Attention's query vectors don't follow that pattern: they hover in a narrow ≈0.10–0.15 band at every level, with no clear crowding effect as the class count grows thirtyfold. Label attention's per-class query mechanism seems to carve out its own consistent notion of "how far apart classes should be," largely independent of how many there are — plain mean pooling's classification head has no such mechanism, and pays for it in geometry as classes multiply.

### Do levels agree on which word matters?

*Method: label-attention weights*

Word attributions across the hierarchy already hinted that different levels can lean on different words for the same description. Here it's quantified across all 200 examples: does the single most-attended word at a coarser level match the single most-attended word at the sub-class level (Label Attention, mean over heads, predicted class)?

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-agreement-hierarchy-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Share of examples where the top-attended word at each level matches the top-attended word at the sub-class level (Label Attention)."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML or lat_la_ml is None:
    print("Label attention artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    def _top_word_ml(lvl, i):
        words = lat_la_ml[f"words_{lvl}"][i]
        row = np.abs(lat_la_ml[f"word_attn_{lvl}"][i][0])
        n = min(len(words), len(row))
        if n == 0:
            return None
        return str(words[int(np.argmax(row[:n]))]).lower()

    _n_ex_lah_ml = len(lat_la_ml["words_sec"])
    _coarser_levels_ml = [l for l in LEVEL_NAMES if l != "sub"]
    agreement_ml = {}
    for lvl in _coarser_levels_ml:
        match, total = 0, 0
        for i in range(_n_ex_lah_ml):
            w_ref, w_lvl = _top_word_ml("sub", i), _top_word_ml(lvl, i)
            if w_ref is not None and w_lvl is not None:
                total += 1
                match += int(w_ref == w_lvl)
        agreement_ml[lvl] = 100 * match / total if total else 0.0

    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(
        x=[LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in _coarser_levels_ml],
        y=[agreement_ml[l] for l in _coarser_levels_ml],
        marker=dict(color="#00BCD4"),
        text=[f"{agreement_ml[l]:.0f}%" for l in _coarser_levels_ml], textposition="outside",
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="Hierarchy level", yaxis_title="Share of examples agreeing with sub-class (%)",
        height=380, yaxis=dict(range=[0, 70]),
    )
    fig.show()
```

The same word tops the ranking at both ends of the hierarchy about **half the time** — 45–49% across section, division, group and class, with no meaningful trend by depth. So the model is neither purely "reusing the same evidence at every level" nor "picking entirely fresh evidence each time": roughly one description in two gets the same star witness for its coarse and fine verdicts, and one in two doesn't — consistent with the geometry finding above, where label attention doesn't obviously reorganise itself level by level either.

### Do confused sections share vocabulary?

*Method: Captum (Integrated Gradients)*

[Top section confusions](#top-section-confusions) found the model confuses **M** with **K** and **J** far more than other section pairs. Does that confusion show up as shared vocabulary — do the top attributed words for M-predicted examples overlap with those for K- or J-predicted examples more than for an unrelated pair of sections?

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-confusion-vocab-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Jaccard overlap between the top-15 attributed words of each section's predicted examples, for the most-confused pairs vs. a random baseline."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML:
    print("Artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    def _section_words_ml(cap, sec_code, top_n=15):
        idx = np.where(np.array([code_of("sec", c) for c in cap["y_pred_sec"]]) == sec_code)[0]
        scores, counts = {}, {}
        for i in idx:
            words = [str(w).lower() for w in cap["words_sec"][i]]
            attn  = np.abs(cap["word_attn_sec"][i][0][:len(words)])
            for w, s in zip(words, attn):
                scores[w] = scores.get(w, 0.0) + float(s)
                counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
        if not scores:
            return set()
        ranked = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1] / counts[kv[0]])
        return set(w for w, _ in ranked[:top_n])

    def _jaccard_ml(a, b):
        return len(a & b) / len(a | b) if a and b else None

    _key_conf_ml  = "labatt" if "labatt" in EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML else EXPLAIN_MODEL_KEYS_ML[0]
    cap_conf_ml   = EXPLAIN_CAPTUM_ML[_key_conf_ml]
    _pred_sec_ml  = np.array([code_of("sec", c) for c in cap_conf_ml["y_pred_sec"]])
    _sections_present_ml = sorted(set(_pred_sec_ml.tolist()))
    _sec_words_ml = {s: _section_words_ml(cap_conf_ml, s) for s in _sections_present_ml}

    CONFUSED_PAIRS_ML = [("M", "K"), ("M", "J"), ("N", "M")]  # from Top section confusions above (unordered, direction doesn't change vocabulary overlap)
    labels_conf_ml, vals_conf_ml = [], []
    for a, b in CONFUSED_PAIRS_ML:
        j = _jaccard_ml(_sec_words_ml.get(a, set()), _sec_words_ml.get(b, set()))
        if j is not None:
            labels_conf_ml.append(f"{a} / {b}")
            vals_conf_ml.append(j)

    rng_conf_ml       = np.random.default_rng(3)
    _confused_codes_ml = {"M", "K", "J", "N"}
    _others_ml        = [s for s in _sections_present_ml if s not in _confused_codes_ml]
    _rand_pairs_ml    = [(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(_others_ml) for b in _others_ml[i + 1:]]
    rng_conf_ml.shuffle(_rand_pairs_ml)
    _baseline_js_ml = [
        j for a, b in _rand_pairs_ml[:10]
        if (j := _jaccard_ml(_sec_words_ml.get(a, set()), _sec_words_ml.get(b, set()))) is not None
    ]
    labels_conf_ml.append("random pairs (mean)")
    vals_conf_ml.append(float(np.mean(_baseline_js_ml)) if _baseline_js_ml else 0.0)

    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(
        x=labels_conf_ml, y=vals_conf_ml,
        marker=dict(color=["#B71C1C"] * (len(labels_conf_ml) - 1) + ["#999999"]),
        text=[f"{v:.3f}" for v in vals_conf_ml], textposition="outside",
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title=None, yaxis_title="Jaccard overlap (top-15 words)",
        height=380, yaxis=dict(range=[0, 0.15]),
    )
    fig.show()
```

Barely at all: the top-15 attributed words for the confused M/K and M/J pairs overlap almost as little (Jaccard ≈ 0.00–0.03) as a random baseline pair of unrelated sections (≈0.01). The model's confusion between these sections isn't explained by them literally keying off the same words — whatever drives M getting mistaken for K or J happens example by example, or through subtler semantic proximity that a top-15-word overlap is too coarse to catch, not through a shared vocabulary visible at the corpus level.

### Do attention heads specialize more at finer levels?

*Method: label-attention weights*

Label attention's 4 heads don't have to agree with each other. Here we ask whether that disagreement is itself a function of hierarchy depth: for the predicted class, how much do the 4 heads' individual "how concentrated is my attention" scores differ from one another, averaged across examples, per level?

```{python}
#| label: fig-explain-head-spec-naf-multilevel
#| fig-cap: "Mean standard deviation, across the 4 attention heads, of each head's top-word attribution share (predicted class), by hierarchy level — higher means the heads behave more differently from one another."

if not HAS_EXPLAIN_LA_ML or lat_la_ml is None:
    print("Label attention artifacts not yet available.")
else:
    def _head_specialization_ml(lvl):
        hw = lat_la_ml[f"head_word_attn_{lvl}"]  # (n_head, k_kept, n_words) per example
        stds = []
        for i in range(len(hw)):
            m = hw[i][:, 0, :]  # (n_head, n_words), predicted class row
            shares = []
            for h in range(m.shape[0]):
                row = np.abs(m[h])
                total = row.sum()
                if total > 0:
                    shares.append(row.max() / total)
            if len(shares) == m.shape[0]:
                stds.append(np.std(shares))
        return float(np.mean(stds)) * 100

    spec_ml = [_head_specialization_ml(lvl) for lvl in LEVEL_NAMES]

    fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
        x=[LEVEL_LABELS_ML[l] for l in LEVEL_NAMES], y=spec_ml,
        mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color="#00BCD4", width=2.5), marker=dict(size=9),
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_title="Hierarchy level", yaxis_title="Std. across heads of top-word share (pp)",
        height=380, yaxis=dict(range=[9, 12.5]),
    )
    fig.show()
```

A small but consistent climb: from 10.6 percentage points at section to 11.4 at sub-class, rising at every step in between. It's a modest effect, not a dramatic one, but it points the same direction as the concentration and geometry findings above: the finer the level, the more room — and apparently the more need — for the 4 heads to carve up the explanation differently from each other, rather than converging on the same handful of words.
